Human hunger can never be satisfied. Human beings also suffer from future hunger. This human being is fame futura famelicus: hungry from hunger that has not yet arrived. That is what distinguishes human hunger from animal hunger: our inability to be satisfied, and our habit of planning ahead for the hunger that will come in the future. Human beings differ from animals through their insatiability. The will to power is only one form of this specifically human inability to be satisfied. Hobbes understood this and made it a foundation of his thought. That is why he is a deeper and more thorough thinker than Nietzsche.
Surely that, too, is a form of nihilism.
But this pereat is almost always tied to a demand for justice that itself appears nihilistic:
Let justice be done, though the world perish.
Every civil servant whose salary is cut;
every worker whose wages are not increased;
every emigrant whose desire for revenge has not yet been satisfied;
every resistance fighter whose compensation claim has not yet been recognized—they all cry:
But here and now, “law and justice” really does mean: let the world perish.

If God is nothing but the Wholly Other of the anti-fascists, then the proof that he exists is that today, in 1952, he is dead.

The soft pillow becomes a fat belly.
The fat belly of 1952 is a soft pillow.
Anyone who denies this denies democracy;
and undermines the sanctuaries of civilization that are now running on empty.

Because he does not mean God.
Because for him—Proudhon in 1840—God is a creation of man.
Only after Feuerbach does Proudhon’s sentence become possible.
For the God made by human beings really was the Deus mortalis—the mortal God.
By 1840 he was already dead in France.
Magnificent, what Günther Krauss says about the sentence homo homini homo in chapter 8, “The Commercial Title in Vitoria”:
“The sentence homo homini homo denies the sentence homo homini lupus—man is a wolf to man.
It denies a real human possibility and a large part of human reality.
This sentence wants to be the final word, but it is not even a first word.
It sounds extremely final, as though the matter were settled, but in reality it not only has no beginning; it actually makes the correct beginning impossible.
The sentence homo homini homo is, if anything, still too optimistic.
The great wars of human beings are not fought against wolves, but against human beings.”
All these tautologies refer to war and can be reduced to the sentence: à la guerre comme à la guerre. In war, war is war. Homo homini homo means no more than that.
